points.text: The constitutional right to litigation gives criminal defendants a full right of defense, including free, uninterfered communication with their defense lawyer. This may be limited by law only if the limit meets the proportionality principle and is specific and clear.

Detained defendants keep the same constitutional rights as others apart from those limited by detention, and since they are cut off from the outside, meetings with their lawyer are the only way to exercise their defense. Monitoring there includes listening and recording, and allowing it regardless of need for the detention purpose or house order goes beyond what is necessary. Merely watching without listening is still acceptable.

Article 28 lets information from monitored lawyer meetings be used as evidence of the charged crime, which harms the defense right to that extent. The invalidity starts on 1 May 1998 to balance the right to litigation with time for authorities to adjust. Any restriction on lawyer-client communication should be decided by a court, with judicial remedies and clear rules.

The detention-house organization rule only describes courts' and prosecutors' supervisory and directing role over detention. It is internal administrative supervision, not authority to monitor or record.
The applicant had been released on bail and the request for a provisional measure did not meet earlier interpretations' standards, so it lacked the required protection of rights and was dismissed.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a prison law rule was unconstitutional that released prisoners who had finished their sentence only on the morning of the day after the sentence ended. The court held that this rule kept people detained after their sentence ended without proper legal procedure and went further than necessary, so it violated the Constitution. Until the rules are fixed, prisoners must be released on the morning of the day their sentence ends.
raw.held: The part of Article 83, paragraph 1 of the Prison Act requiring release on the morning after the sentence ends conflicts with Articles 8 and 23 of the Constitution, and that part loses effect from 1 June 2010. Until the rules are amended, prisoners must be released on the morning of the day their sentence ends; the request for a temporary order was rejected.

points.text: Under Article 8 of the Constitution, any measure restricting personal liberty needs a legal basis and proper legal procedure, and must also meet Article 23.

The next-morning release rule began as a practical arrangement because of night-time work and transport difficulties, but the sentence period should be counted so that it ends at the end of its last day, and after that prisoners should be released unless another constitutional legal ground exists.
The state's power to punish ends when the sentence is served, so holding people longer is like punishment, and the rule set no proper legal procedure for it, violating Article 8.

The aim of protecting prisoners' transport and safety is legitimate, but release in the morning of the final day is possible without those concerns, so the delay is not necessary and breaches proportionality under Article 23.
The temporary order request was rejected because the ruling itself already decided the case, making such an order unnecessary.

who: Agencies that must revise the release rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether two tax rules were constitutional. They required companies to move expenses or losses that were recorded as owed but still unpaid after two years into 'other income', which raised the company's taxable income. The court held that the rules go beyond what the Income Tax Act authorizes and violate the constitutional principle that taxes must be set by law.
raw.held: The two rules, which required unpaid expenses or losses older than two years to be turned into other income, violate Article 19 of the Constitution because they exceed the authority the Income Tax Act gave. They lose effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Under Article 19, the key elements of a tax, such as who is taxed, what is taxed, the tax base and the rate, must be set by law or by an order clearly authorized by law. Only minor detail or technical matters may be left to agency orders.

The Income Tax Act sets the accounting basis and the way income is calculated, but it does not say that unpaid expenses must become other income after a set period regardless of whether the debt has ended. Turning expenses into income affects the tax base, so the principle that taxes must be set by law applies.

Forcing companies to turn unpaid expenses older than two years into income raises their income and tax for that year and may cause financial difficulty that affects their business. It is therefore not a minor or technical matter.
Adding a two-year limit by administrative order is also inconsistent with the Civil Code's rules on extinction by limitation, as far as interest is concerned.

The authorizing provisions of the Income Tax Act only give the agency a basis to make enforcement rules and audit rules. They do not clearly authorize the Ministry of Finance to turn unpaid expenses into other income, so the rules create a tax burden the law does not contain.

who: Companies with long-unpaid recorded expenses or losses

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Telecommunications Act is unconstitutional in requiring government approval before anyone uses radio frequencies, and in punishing unapproved use with criminal penalties and confiscation of equipment. The court decided these rules do not violate the proportionality principle, free speech, or property rights. It also noted that the government should allocate frequencies fairly and review its rules as technology advances.
raw.held: The provisions requiring approval to use radio frequencies, punishing unapproved use, and confiscating the equipment used are consistent with the proportionality principle, free speech (Article 11) and property rights (Article 15).

points.text: Free speech includes freedom of communication, such as using radio and broadcasting, but it is not absolute and the state may limit it by law within the bounds of Article 23.
Radio frequencies are a public resource of all citizens, so requiring prior approval serves the legitimate aim of preventing interference and protecting orderly, safe radio use.
The approval requirement is a necessary and helpful means to that aim, so it is proportionate and does not violate free speech.
The legislature judged that administrative fines would not be enough to stop unlicensed use, so criminal penalties (detention and/or a fine) were not disproportionate.

Confiscating the equipment, whether or not it belongs to the offender, helps prevent repeat illegal use, and such radio equipment is controlled material, so confiscation does not go beyond what is necessary or violate property rights.
The state should distribute frequencies fairly and reasonably, and the authority should review its rules in step with technological progress.

who: People who want to use radio frequencies
People who use frequencies without approval

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter ruling was constitutional when it said that government subsidies paid to bus and ship operators for running remote or public-service routes at a loss must be taxed as business tax. The court decided the ruling went beyond what the business tax law provides and imposed a tax duty the law does not set out. It therefore conflicts with the Constitution and may not be applied.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1997 letter ruling, which taxed loss-making subsidies paid to bus and ship passenger operators on remote or service routes, went beyond the 1985 business tax law and conflicts with Article 19 of the Constitution. It must not be applied.

points.text: Article 19 of the Constitution means that tax duties and tax breaks, including who is taxed, what is taxed, the tax base and the rate, must be set by law or by a order clearly authorized by law.
Under the old business tax law, tax applies to selling goods or services, and selling services means providing services to others and receiving payment for it.

The Ministry's ruling treated the subsidies as payment for transport services, but under the transport subsidy rules the subsidy is an administrative payment by the transport authority to cover the gap between ticket income and operating cost, in the public interest of promoting mass transit.

Because the subsidized operators do not sell services to the transport authority, the subsidies are not the kind of payment counted as sales under the business tax law and fall outside its taxable scope.
The ruling therefore went beyond the law and created a business tax duty the law does not provide, which conflicts with Article 19 and means it cannot be applied.
The part of the request about a Supreme Administrative Court order was not accepted, because that order only dismissed a retrial request on procedural grounds and did not apply the ruling.

who: Bus and ship passenger transport operators
Operators on remote or service routes receiving subsidies
Ministry of Finance and tax authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the enforcement regulations of the Civil Servant Retirement Act was unconstitutional. The rule combined the earlier retirement or severance benefits of people who returned to public service with their new benefits, and capped the total at the Act's maximum. The court held that the rule lacked clear authorization in a statute and added limits the law does not contain, so it violates the constitution's principle that such matters must be set by law.
raw.held: Article 13, paragraph 2 of the enforcement regulations violates the legal reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution. It will lose effect no later than two years after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Counting retirement years, including years after returning to service and the cap on them, greatly affects pension claims and public finances, so it must be set by law. A regulation may only cover minor, technical details and may not add limits the law does not contain.

The Act's provisions on benefit bases and the 35-year maximum, and on combining service before and after the Act's amendment, do not clearly say whether a returning retiree's new years are combined with earlier ones. Nor can an intent to let the agency decide this by regulation be inferred.
The Act's Article 13 says service before retirement is not counted when a retiree returns and retires again, so the two periods are counted separately.

The regulation combines earlier and later service and applies the maximum cap. Although meant to keep years counting fair, no provision of the Act supports it, so it lacks clear authorization. It deals with matters reserved to law and restricts returning employees' pension claims beyond the law.

Redesigning the rules for retirees who return to service involves many factors and needs time. The authorities must review and amend the laws within two years, and if they do not, the regulation lapses.

who: Retired civil servants who returned to public service
Agencies responsible for the retirement law

raw.answer: The case asked whether a tax law rule is unconstitutional that says serving a tax assessment on just one joint owner of jointly held property counts as serving all of them. The court decided that, for tax assessment decisions, this rule fails the constitutional requirement of due legal process and harms the appeal and court rights of owners who were never served. The rule will lose effect no later than two years after the ruling is published.
raw.held: Article 19, paragraph 3 of the Tax Collection Act is contrary to Article 16 of the Constitution to the extent that serving one joint owner is treated as serving all on tax assessment decisions. That part loses effect no later than two years from the ruling's publication date.

points.text: Property rights and the rights to administrative appeal and court action are protected by the Constitution. Serving a tax assessment notice affects property and lets people learn of the decision so they can challenge it.
The rule aims at public interests such as lower collection costs and greater efficiency, since joint owners can be numerous and scattered and hard to serve individually.
Due administrative process requires tax authorities to investigate who the affected people are and to let those identified know of the decision so they can challenge it.

Under the rule, the time limit to seek review for an unserved owner runs from when another owner was served. That owner may never learn of the assessment, and the limit cannot be extended once missed, so the rule seriously harms their appeal and court rights.
Even where an address is unknown, authorities can use public notice or other low-cost methods, so removing the right to be served goes beyond what is necessary.
Because replacing individual service involves balancing appeal rights, costs and efficiency, and needs time to plan, the rule stays valid for up to two years.

who: Joint owners not served with a tax assessment
Joint owners of property such as ancestral worship trusts

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 107 of the Land Registration Rules, as amended on 14 September 2001, was unconstitutional. The rule deals with a mortgage that one co-owner placed on their share of jointly owned land when the land is later divided. The court decided the rule is consistent with the civil law and does not conflict with the constitutional protection of property rights.
raw.held: The court held that Article 107 of the Land Registration Rules, as amended on 14 September 2001, accords with the civil law's intent and does not conflict with Article 15 of the Constitution protecting property rights.

points.text: Article 15 protects people's ability to use, benefit from and dispose of their property as it stands, and this must not be harmed by other people's legal acts.

A co-owner's share is like ownership itself, and the co-owner may freely dispose of it, including by mortgaging it. A mortgage is also protected property. A co-owner can set one up alone, so it fits the constitution if setting it up and enforcing it does not harm the other co-owners.
A mortgage on a co-owner's share is not affected when the jointly owned property is later divided.

Under the rule, if the mortgagee did not agree beforehand, the mortgage is carried over to each parcel after division. This protects the mortgagee from loss, but it also puts a mortgage burden on the other co-owners' parcels.

Even so, what is mortgaged is still the share in the original jointly owned property. After division, the object of the mortgage is the carried-over shares on each parcel, and in enforcement those shares are what is auctioned.

After an auction, the buyer and the other co-owners hold the whole property jointly again. The other co-owners regain their pre-division shares and the carried-over mortgage ends because it was enforced, which protects both the other co-owners and the mortgagee.

raw.answer: The case asked whether two government rules were unconstitutional because they stopped certain odd-shaped urban plots (fragmentary land, or 畸零地) from being taxed under the lighter farmland tax. The court decided that the rules added a requirement the law does not contain, and so violated the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on statute. The parts of the rules that conflict with this ruling can no longer be applied from the day it was announced.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance letter and the Ministry of the Interior order, as they apply to urban fragmentary plots that cannot legally be built on and are still used for farming, add requirements the law lacks and violate Article 19 of the Constitution. The parts inconsistent with the ruling are no longer to be applied from its announcement date.

points.text: Article 19 of the Constitution requires the main elements of a tax duty or tax relief to be set out clearly in a statute. Agencies interpreting the law must stay within the legal interpretation and may not create tax duties the law does not contain.

Urban land with set land values would normally pay land value tax. But urban land that legally cannot be built on and is still farmed pays the generally lighter farmland tax, because its income is limited and the aim is to ease farmers' burden.
The land tax law and the Equalization of Land Rights Act do not define 'legally cannot be built on' and do not clearly authorize agencies to define it by order.

Under the Building Act article 44, a fragmentary plot cannot be built on alone until it is merged with neighboring land to meet the minimum size. Before merger it therefore counts as legally unbuildable, and if it is still farmed it should pay the farmland tax.

The two government rules, which deny this treatment because merger by agreement is still possible or because the land cannot be built on alone, went beyond the limits of legal interpretation. They added requirements the statutes lack and so violate the principle that taxes must rest on statute.
The request about another 1976 Ministry of Finance letter was not accepted, because the applicant did not specify how it infringed constitutionally protected rights.

who: Owners of urban fragmentary plots still used for farming
Taxpayers paying land value tax or farmland tax
Ministry of Finance and Ministry of the Interior

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule requiring the labor insurance provider to pay cash benefits within ten days of receiving an application is unconstitutional, because it does not add late-payment interest when the deadline is missed. The court found the rule consistent with the constitution's policy of protecting workers. It said only that the legislature has freedom to decide how workers harmed by the insurer's delay can get a remedy, and should keep reviewing this.
raw.held: The 1996 rule requiring the insurer to pay complete, approved cash benefit claims within ten days of receiving the application is held to fit the constitution's basic policy of protecting workers.

points.text: The constitution tells the state to protect workers and to run social insurance, so the state should set up an insurance system where workers share risks.
The legislature made the Labor Insurance Act so workers can quickly get benefits when an insured event happens, protecting their livelihood.
The ten-day payment rule pushes the insurer to finish cash payments quickly, protecting workers or their beneficiaries after an insured event, so it does not conflict with the constitutional policy.
How workers harmed by an insurer's blameworthy delay get relief is left to the legislature's free choice.

The legislature should still review worker protection from time to time, considering social security developments, other social insurance, and the existing late-fee and benefit-suspension rule in Article 17 of the Act.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in Taiwan's Wrongful Imprisonment Compensation Act is constitutional. The rule denied any compensation to people who were later acquitted if their own intentional or grossly negligent conduct led to their detention. The court held that this blanket denial violates the constitutional proportionality principle, and the rule will lose effect within two years unless it is revised.
raw.held: Article 2, item 3 of the Act, as applied to detention under the cited Code of Criminal Procedure and Military Trial Act provisions, is unconstitutional because it bars all compensation in every such case. It will lose effect two years from the announcement unless the authorities revise it by then.

points.text: People whose liberty is restricted for the public interest, such as by detention, and who bear a burden beyond what is normally tolerable have a right to reasonable compensation. This follows from the constitutional protection of physical liberty and equality.

Compensation under the Act is not based on a public official's fault. It is a criminal-justice compensation paid in money for a special sacrifice caused by the state's exercise of its punishment power.

The law may reduce or exclude compensation where the person is to blame for the loss, in order to avoid improper or excessive payouts. But this must be necessary to that aim to satisfy the proportionality principle.

The rule does not consider whether the person's conduct was suspected of meeting the elements of a crime or instead obstructed or misled the investigation or trial. It also ignores how blameworthy the conduct was and how large the loss was, and it excludes all compensation in every case. That is not necessary to prevent improper or excessive payouts, so it violates proportionality.

The relevant authorities have two years to review the rule and decide whether and how to limit compensation, fully or partly. They must base this on the person's conduct, their degree of blame and their loss. If they do not act in time, the rule loses effect.

who: People whose own conduct led to their detention
Legislators and authorities who must revise the Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional that Taiwan's appeals and administrative litigation laws do not say that a document left at a depository (deposit service) only takes effect 10 days after deposit. The court decided this is not unconstitutional: service takes effect once the deposit procedure is completed. It also suggested that the authorities review the service rules over time.
raw.held: The Appeals Act rule applying the Administrative Litigation Act's deposit-service provision, under which deposit service takes effect when service is legally completed, does not violate the constitutional protection of the right to appeal and to sue.

points.text: The right to petition for review and to sue is protected by the Constitution, and the procedures behind it must meet due process, judged by factors such as the interests at stake and the public interest.

Service aims to make sure people actually know of a document or are in a position to know. Deposit service follows set steps, with notices posted and left nearby, and documents kept three months, so the purpose of service is achieved.

People give their addresses when they file, deposit service is used only when ordinary service fails, and the procedure is fairly strict. Effect at completion also supports speedy proceedings and the public interest, so it meets due process.

The two kinds of litigation differ in purpose and nature, so they need not have identical rules. A 10-day wait could even treat people who collect the document at once unequally, and people can name a service agent or take other steps if they will be away.
How long before deposit service takes effect is a policy choice for the legislature, so lacking the civil procedure's 10-day rule does not violate equality.

Although the rule is constitutional, the civil procedure's 10-day rule gives better protection, so the authorities should review service rules to fit modern life and work conditions and the legal system's coherence.
